newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S.-connected Kurds set for exodus from Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-connected Kurds set for exodus from Iraq.

text.p: The evacuation of hundreds of Kurds who worked for the United States in northern Iraq was set to begin on Sunday to Turkey in the first step in a long journey to America as refugees, Kurdish officials said.

"We received an approved list from the Americans and we expect the first evacuations could occur around noon today (0800 GMT), a Kurdish official who asked not to be identified said in the border town of Zakho.
"I don't think the evacuations will be completed today. There will probably be some tomorrow as well," he said.
As many as 2,500 Iraqi Kurds are expected to be relocated to a camp in the Turkish town of Silopi where they will be processed for asylum in the United States.
Most worked as employees of U.S. aid programmes in northern Iraq but some are believed to have been engaged in intelligence activities for the Americans as well.

All have been deemed to be at risk from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein who is viewed in the region as newly resurgent after having helped one Kurdish faction defeat another one two weeks ago in the city of Arbil.
Among those expected to be ferried out, either by bus or helicopter, are adminstrators, drivers, messengers and their families.
About 250 members of the Iraqi National Congress, a U.S.-funded group dedicated to the overthrow of Saddam, are also set to cross the border in the next few days.

Reliable information about the evacuation has been difficult to come by since all U.S. citizens in government programmes in Iraqi Kurdistan were evacuated shortly after the fighting broke out in Arbil on August 31.

Hundreds of Kurds who have been expecting evacuation since then have been holed up in small hotels and private residences across northern Iraq, anxiously awaiting word as they cope with searing heat, restless children and boredom.

"The last 10 days have been like 10 years," said Moyyad, who has been waiting in a house with 17 other people in Dohuk, about 50 km (30 miles) south of the Turkish border, expecting to cross to Silopi and then on to America.
"The chidren are naughty, my wife is sick and I have been smoking three packs of cigarettes a day and feeling chest pains. All of this is from the strain."

One Kurd in Zakho who received a telephone call on Sunday morning notifying him the evacuation was about to get under way said he was told not to bring weapons, radios, televisions, computers or typewriters to the border.
"They told us just to bring one suitcase with personal belongings," he said.
The Washington Post said on Sunday that the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency had spent about $100 million since 1991 to oust Saddam, with very little to show for its efforts.

The paper said the CIA had funded dissident Kurds and Iraqis, enabling them to buy light arms and ammunition, communications gear, publishing materials, broadcasting equipment, cars, trucks, food and medicine.

Officials of the Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which now controls virtually all of northern Iraq, are reluctant to see so many of the region's skilled people leave and have played down the need for the departures.
However, KDP forces have agreed to provide transport and security to the border for all those who want to go and whom the U.S. government is willing to take.
